records.name_note: NC State's dedicated page lists Calathea ornata and Maranta ornata under 'Previously known as:', and its Cultivars / Varieties entries 'Albolineata', 'Beauty Star', 'Roseolineata' and 'Sanderiana' are cultivar names that supply no species field. NC State's page-title parenthetical reads 'Pinstripe Calathea, Pinstripe Plant', and its Common Name(s) list is alphabetized and shows the same two names in the same order. records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Plant Toolbox page for Goeppertia ornata carries the tags "non-toxic for cats" and "non-toxic for dogs" in its Tags line, scoped to cats and dogs only. The full Tags line reads '#partial shade tolerant #non-toxic for cats #houseplant #herbaceous perennial #tropical #humidity tolerant #container plant #non-toxic for dogs #evergreen #white flowers #interesting leaves #variegated'. NC State Plant Type: Houseplant, Perennial. The page has no Poison block, no poison-part list, no symptom list, no handling warning and no horse tag, and it states nothing about toxicity to humans or any other animal. RHS's dedicated page carries no toxicity entry, and no admissible source addresses eating the plant.
unknowns: NC State and RHS both have dedicated pages for Goeppertia ornata. RHS's Botanical Details Name Status reads 'Correct', which corroborates scientific_name_accepted. MoBot and UF/IFAS were unreachable or unlocated, and Clemson HGIC had no page for it. RHS's Cultivation paragraph opens with genus-wide text ('Under glass grow in peat-free potting compost in bright indirect or filtered light. Provide high humidity, draught-free conditions and a constant temperature of at least 16°C.', near-identical on RHS's Goeppertia zebrina profile), so it supplies no field.

Mature size comes from NC State's species Dimensions block, 'Height: 1 ft. 0 in. - 3 ft. 0 in.' and 'Width: 1 ft. 0 in. - 3 ft. 0 in.' (12-36 in each). RHS gives Max Height '0.5-1 metres' (19.7-39.4 in) and a narrower Max Spread '0.1-0.5 metres' (3.9-19.7 in), and its description says 'to 90cm tall'. NC State's species-specific block is the anchor. The cultivar 'Beauty Star' figure ('up to 2 feet tall') is not the species' and is not used.

Temperature: NC State's room-temperature range of 65 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit is not split into day and night; it is mapped to the day fields, and night_f_* stay null. No chill-damage onset is stated: NC State's USDA zones (11a, 11b, 12a, 12b) and RHS's H1A are hardiness ratings, and RHS's 'constant temperature of at least 16°C' is genus-wide Cultivation text, so chill_damage_f stays null.
Humidity: NC State says 'the humidity about 60%', a single approximate figure. It is recorded as humidity_pct_min only, with no maximum.

Light: NC State's prose says 'bright, indirect light or partial shade' and gives no foot-candle figure. Its only hour figure ('2-6 hours') is the site-wide legend inside the structured Light value 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', so light_fc_min, light_fc_good and direct_sun_hours_max stay null. outdoor_sun_exposure is part_shade, from NC State's structured Light field and RHS's Position field ('Partial shade'). NC State's warning that browning leaves may come from 'too much direct sun' excludes full_sun and part_sun.

Watering: 'Avoid overwatering or allowing the soil to dry out' was read as keep_moist; it also warns that overwatering can cause root rot, so it could be read as between keep_moist and keep_barely_moist. No numeric watering interval is given.

Soil: the 'African violets or peat-based mix' wording is an either/or; african_violet was taken from the first named mix. Soil pH: NC State's Soil pH field reads 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)', but RHS's pH field reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', so the Neutral band's bounds are not used and soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max stay null.

Fertilizing: the page says 'fertilization monthly during the growing season with a balanced liquid fertilizer'. This is a word-based cadence with no stated day count, no months and no dilution fraction, so interval, months and strength are null.
Edibility, pollination/attracts and any human or other-animal toxicity are not addressed by the page, so these are null.

records.name_note: Two admissible sources have a dedicated page for this taxon. RHS's Goeppertia roseopicta profile renders 'rose-painted calathea' as the common name beneath its H1 and lists 'Jungle rose' under Other common names; its Synonyms field lists Calathea roseopicta and Calathea 'Roseo Picta'. NC State's Goeppertia roseopicta page renders an alphabetized Common Name(s) list (Jungle Rose, Rose Painted Calathea, Rose-Painted Calathea), in the same order as its page-title parenthetical, and its description opens 'Rose-painted Calathea is a colorful evergreen perennial'. NC State lists Calathea roseopicta and Maranta roseopicta under 'Previously known as'. Rose-Painted Calathea is RHS's lead name and NC State's description opener, so it is used rather than Jungle Rose; this catalog already uses the bare name Calathea for Goeppertia orbifolia.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Tags line for Goeppertia roseopicta reads in full: '#partial shade tolerant #perennial #showy leaves #houseplant #humidity tolerant #interesting leaves #container plant #wet soils intolerant #tropical evergreen #evergreen perenial #non-toxic for cats #variegated #green leaves #non-toxic for dogs'. The cat and dog scoping comes from its '#non-toxic for cats' and '#non-toxic for dogs' tags; no other animal is tagged. The NC State page carries no Poison block, so there is no human-scoped severity rating, poison-part list, symptom list or handling warning. NC State Plant Type: Herbaceous Perennial, Houseplant. RHS's dedicated Goeppertia roseopicta profile (plant 357231) carries no toxicity entry, and neither dedicated page addresses eating the plant, so the sources show no disagreement on scope or edibility.
unknowns: Two admissible sources have a dedicated page for Goeppertia roseopicta: NC State (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/goeppertia-roseopicta/) and RHS (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/357231/goeppertia-roseopicta/details). RHS's Cultivation paragraph ('Under glass grow in peat-free potting compost with bright indirect or filtered light. Provide high humidity, draught-free conditions and a constant temperature of at least 16°C. Water moderately when in growth and keep just moist in winter. Apply a balanced liquid fertiliser monthly') is character-identical on RHS's Goeppertia insignis profile (plant 386634), so it is genus-wide text and supplies no field. RHS's structured Position field ('Partial shade') agrees with NC State's Light field, and its Moisture field ('Moist but well–drained or Well–drained') is consistent with moderate drainage. Size conflict: RHS gives Max Height and Max Spread of 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in) and describes 'A clump-forming perennial to 25cm', against NC State's 1 to 2 feet (12-24 in); NC State's species Dimensions block is the anchor. MoBot and plantfinder.mobot.org did not load, EDIS did not load, and Clemson returned 403.

Cultivation note, not a toxicity claim: NC State's description says to avoid tap water because it contains fluoride and will cause the foliage to turn brown, and recommends rain water or distilled water.

NC State's description also says brown leaves and tips can result from low humidity or fluoride in the tap water; curling leaves result from low humidity or inadequate watering; bright coloring fades in inadequate light, and direct sunlight can cause leaf scorch.
night_f_min and night_f_max are null: NC State gives a single room-temperature range (65 to 75 F) with no separate night figure. It is recorded as day_f_min/day_f_max only.
chill_damage_f is null: no admissible source states a damage-onset temperature. NC State's USDA zone list (11a-12b) is a hardiness rating, not an onset figure.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State's prose says only 'slightly acidic pH', and its structured Soil pH field lists the open-ended Acid (<6.0) band plus Neutral (6.0-8.0), so no floor can be read off it; RHS's pH field reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', listing alkaline soils as acceptable, so no ceiling can be taken from NC State's Neutral band either.

water_regime and the watering fields are null: NC State gives no watering cadence. Its soil-moisture target sits in a soil-amendment sentence ('Add vermiculite or perlite to improve the soils drainage since the soil should be moist but not soggy or wet.'), its structured Soil Drainage field values are Good Drainage and Moist, and its one watering instruction concerns water quality ('Water the plant with rain water or distilled water.'). Its problems text warns 'Overwatering can cause root rot' and says curling leaves can result from 'inadequate watering'. No numeric watering interval is given. RHS's Cultivation watering line ('Water moderately when in growth and keep just moist in winter') is genus-wide text, identical on RHS's Goeppertia insignis profile, and is not used.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months and fertilize_strength are null: NC State says 'once a month during its growing season, spring through summer'. That is a word-based cadence with named seasons, and no dilution strength is stated.

direct_sun_hours_max is null: the only hour figure (2-6 hours) is in the structured Light field's category legend, not species-specific prose. light_fc_min and light_fc_good are null: the page gives 'bright, indirect light' with no foot-candle figures.
outdoor_sun_exposure is part_shade only, from NC State's 'Partial Shade' Light field. The plant is a tropical houseplant (zones 11a-12b), so outdoor exposure is of limited relevance.
humidity_pct_max is null: NC State says only that humidity 'should be above 60%'.
is_edible and attracts_pollinators are null: NC State does not address eating or pollinators. Its Attracts field is absent.

NC State lists cultivars 'Cynthia', 'Dottie', 'Medallion', 'Rosy' and 'Surprise Star'. No cultivar text was used for any field. No text from the separate Goeppertia veitchiana (Medallion Calathea) page, nor from the landed makoyana or insignis records, was used.
NC State's Life Cycle field says Biennial while its description says evergreen perennial. Neither is used in a field.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated page has the binomial Philodendron xanadu as its H1; its Common Name(s) list is alphabetized, Winterbourn Philodendron then Xanadu Philodendron, in the same order as its page-title parenthetical, and its Description opens with 'Xanadu philodendron'. RHS's dedicated Philodendron xanadu page gives Name Status Correct, lists Philodendron 'Xanadu' [2] as a synonym and renders no common name. UF/IFAS's fact sheet writes the plant as Philodendron x 'Xanadu', a hybrid notation that NC State and RHS do not use, and gives the common name 'Xanadu' philodendron; the given name is kept unchanged. Xanadu Philodendron is landed because NC State's Description and UF/IFAS's common-name field lead with it, and Winterbourn Philodendron is recorded as an alias. NC State's Previously known as list carries Philodendron 'Xanadu' and Thaumatophyllum xanadu; the Thaumatophyllum entry is the same change this catalog followed for the landed Horsehead Philodendron, whose NC State page lists Thaumatophyllum bipinnatifidum the same way, so the accepted name is Philodendron xanadu. NC State says the plant is sometimes given the cultivar name 'Winterbourn', that this cultivar name has not been registered with the International Aroid Society, and that plants with this name appear to have no features that distinguish the cultivar from the species, so Winterbourn is not treated as a separate plant here. RHS, by contrast, keeps Philodendron 'Winterbourn' as an Accepted cultivar name on its own page, with Philodendron 'Xanadu' [1] and Philodendron [Xanadu] as synonyms; nothing is taken from that cultivar page. This record is kept apart from the landed Horsehead Philodendron, hederaceum and erubescens records.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's dedicated Philodendron xanadu page and RHS's dedicated Philodendron xanadu page both address toxicity. On NC State, the block headed 'Poisonous to Humans:' is human-scoped and gives Poison Severity Low, Poison Symptoms 'If the leaves or stems are eaten or chewed, swelling of the lips, tongue, and mouth can occur. It may also cause mouth pain and drooling. The sap can cause skin irritation.', Poison Toxic Principle Calcium oxalate, Causes Contact Dermatitis Yes, and a Poison Part list of seven values: Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems. The symptom sentence names leaves or stems while the Poison Part list names seven parts; the page does not reconcile the two. A banner above the Description reads 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics.' The Low rating belongs to the human-scoped block and is not a pet rating. Separately, NC State's Problems field carries four stacked tags, Contact Dermatitis, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children and Problem for Dogs; the Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags support toxic_to_pets, and the page gives no pet-specific symptom list or severity. NC State's Plant Type field lists three values: Herbaceous Perennial, Houseplant, Poisonous. The calcium-oxalate ingestion toxicity is distinct from the sap skin-irritation warning (Causes Contact Dermatitis Yes; 'The sap can cause skin irritation.'), which is a handling hazard. RHS's Potentially harmful field reads 'Harmful if eaten; skin/eye irritant/allergen. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling'. Its pet line reads 'Pets: Harmful if eaten; skin/eye irritant/allergen' and names no animal, so the two sources differ in scope and only NC State names cats and dogs. No source states any edibility use.
unknowns: NC State's dedicated Philodendron xanadu page is the main source. RHS also has a dedicated Philodendron xanadu page (Name Status Correct, synonym Philodendron 'Xanadu' [2]), and UF/IFAS covers the plant in EDIS fact sheet FP474 under the name Philodendron x 'Xanadu'; their naming, light and Potentially harmful fields are cited where used. RHS's Cultivation paragraph is Philodendron genus text, word for word the same on RHS's Philodendron bipinnatifidum page apart from the spelling of fertiliser, so its watering, feeding and misting advice supplies no field. Mature size follows NC State's species Dimensions block (3 to 5 ft tall and wide); RHS gives Max Height 1-1.5 metres (39 to 59 in) and Max Spread 1.5-2.5 metres (59 to 98 in), and UF/IFAS gives Height 2 to 4 feet and Spread 4 to 6 feet, so the sources disagree, mostly on spread. Missouri Botanical Garden's only match is the cultivar page Philodendron 'Winterbourn' XANADU, which could not be loaded here and would supply no species field in any case. Clemson's only match is its Philodendron, Pothos and Monstera fact sheet, and no Penn State, UMD or UGA dedicated page was found. Nothing is borrowed from the Philodendron genus or sibling species.

NC State's Light field lists Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day) and Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours), and its prose says the plant, if planted outdoors, prefers full sun to partial shade, while indoors it prefers bright but indirect light. RHS's dedicated page gives Position Partial shade only, and UF/IFAS's fact sheet for Philodendron x 'Xanadu' gives Light requirement: plant grows in the shade and says the plant is well adapted to the shade of tall trees. Full sun is listed by NC State alone and excluded by both other sources' structured light fields, so full_sun is left out; part_shade, listed by NC State and RHS, is kept. UF/IFAS's shade-only value is likewise excluded by the other two, so full_shade is not added. outdoor_sun_exposure is an outdoor landscape value, not an indoor light recommendation. direct_sun_hours_max is left null because the only hour figures are NC State's generic light-category ranges.

Indoors, the page says 'temperature ranges of 65 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit' without separating day from night, so day_f and night_f fields are left null. chill_damage_f is null: the page gives only a hardiness range (zones 9b to 11b), which is not a damage-onset temperature. No cool-rest guidance.
Humidity is only described as 'some humidity' with no percentage or low/average/high level, so humidity_need and the percentages are null.

Watering: the page says only that 'Yellowing of the leaves will occur if overwatered' and 'overwatering should be avoided', and gives a structured Soil Drainage value of Moist. records.toxicity_detail: NC State (plants.ces.ncsu.edu, dedicated T. fluminensis page): top-of-page statement "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." The Poison Severity (Low) sits in the page's "Poisonous to Humans" block, so it is a human-scoped rating, not a cat or dog rating. Poison Symptoms as the page words them: "If ingested by pets or humans, it can mouth and stomach irritation, vomiting, swelling of the mouth, and difficulty breathing. It can also cause skin redness and irritation." Poison Toxic Principle: unknown. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part (full list): Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems. Problems list (full): Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses, Weedy. The ingestion toxicity to cats, dogs and horses is carried by the separate Problem for Cats / Dogs / Horses tags (page tags "#problem for dogs #problem for horses #problem for cats"), which is a different matter from the skin-irritation warning: "Contact with the plant can cause skin redness and irritation. Wear protective gloves when handling this plant." Prose: "This species is mildly toxic to pets and humans if ingested." Plant Type values as rendered (5): Ground Cover, Herbaceous Perennial, Houseplant, Perennial, Poisonous. RHS (rhs.org.uk dedicated page) separately says "Contact with foliage may irritate skin" and is silent on ingestion.
unknowns: Cultivation caution (not a schema field): NC State says 'Considered an invasive species, noxious weed, or pest plant in many locations. Seriously affected areas include Australia, New Zealand, and the southeastern United States.' and that outdoors it 'will root at each node and can become invasive'; it also tags the plant weedy and aggressive.

NC State: 'This species prefers bright, indirect sun and moist, well-drained soil or potting mix. It can be grown in full sun, but it needs afternoon protection to prevent leaf scorch.' MoBot: 'Best in filtered sun. Will grow in direct sun with some afternoon protection. Also grows in shade.' RHS's Position field lists Partial shade only, and its Cultivation says 'Place in bright, filtered light but not direct sunlight.' RHS rates T. zebrina, T. pallida and T. spathacea 'Full sun, Partial shade' on their own pages, so the Partial-shade-only rating is specific to this species.

records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox page for Chamaedorea seifrizii. Under the "Poisonous to Humans:" heading (a human-scoped block) the page gives Poison Severity: Low (the page banner also reads "This plant has low severity poison characteristics."); Poison Symptoms: "The fruit's flesh is irritating to the skin if handled by sensitive people."; Poison Toxic Principle: Oxalic acid; Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes; Poison Part: Fruits (the only part listed). The Problems tag list on the page carries "Contact Dermatitis" and no other tag; there is no Problem for Cats and no Problem for Dogs tag, and no cat or dog statement anywhere on the page. Fruit Description also says: "Round, bluish-black fruits. The flesh is irritating if touched." Plant Type values on the page: Houseplant, Perennial, Shrub. This is a handling (skin-contact) warning about the fruit flesh, not a documented ingestion toxicity or pet toxicity; the severity rating comes from NC State's human-scoped Poison block, not from any pet tag.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: no admissible source read names this species with cats or dogs. NC State's only toxicity content is the human-scoped Poison block (handling warning, oxalic acid, Contact Dermatitis Yes, Poison Part Fruits) and has no Problem for Cats or Problem for Dogs tag.

is_edible left null: no read source states this palm, or a part of it, is used for food or is not edible; the NC State fruit-flesh handling warning is a skin-irritation statement, not an edibility statement.
attracts_pollinators left null: the NC State page for this exact species has no Attracts field and no Landscape Theme field, and no unconditional pollinator statement.

NC State and UF/IFAS have dedicated pages for this exact taxon; UF/IFAS's is fact sheet FPS120 (https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/FP120). RHS has no page for Chamaedorea seifrizii (its plant URL returned 404 and its search page listed none), so no RHS Name Status, pH, size or hardiness data exist. Missouri Botanical Garden (plantfinder.mobot.org) refused non-browser fetches here and was not read. Clemson HGIC returned 403. The other UF/IFAS pages found (Palms as Houseplants, ENH21, ENH854) are multi-species pages and were not used for taxon-specific fields.

scientific_name_accepted rests on the binomial of NC State's dedicated page; UF/IFAS's dedicated FPS120 page gives the same name ("Scientific name: Chamaedorea seifrizii"). water_regime is keep_barely_moist from NC State's prose 'slightly moist potting mix' plus the overwatering root-rot warning; no source gives a dry-down depth, watering interval or watering statement beyond that. soil_base standard_potting is read from NC State's 'potting mix' / 'potting medium must be well-drained' prose; no source names a specific mix.

UF/IFAS's FPS120 Light requirement field reads 'plant grows in the shade', and its prose says 'Bamboo palm should be planted in a shaded location on well-drained soil.'

Temperature, chill damage, humidity percentages, numeric soil pH, fertilizing and a cool-rest period have no admissible source for this exact species. UF/IFAS's Soil tolerances line reads 'acidic; slightly alkaline; clay; sand; loam', with no pH figures. NC State's USDA zone 10a-12b rating (UF/IFAS gives 10A through 11B) is a hardiness range, not a chill-damage onset temperature.
NC State's page carries both a low-severity banner and a Poison Severity of Low; the Poison block is human-scoped and its only symptom text is a skin-contact handling warning.

UF/IFAS's FPS120 reads "Invasive potential: not known to be invasive" and adds "Although currently classified as “not a problem species,” this plant was listed as invasive on the UF/IFAS Assessment in the past."

records.name_note: Admissible dedicated pages split on the lead name. RHS's profile renders Arabian coffee beneath its H1 (page title "Coffea arabica | Arabian coffee") and lists arabica coffee, coffee under Other common names. NC State's page-title parenthetical reads "(Arabian Coffee, Coffee, Coffee Plant)", an alphabetized list whose order matches the Common Name(s) list on the page, and its Description opens "The coffee plant is a small, broadleaf evergreen shrub or small tree in the coffee family (Rubiaceae) with an upright habit." UF/IFAS's fact sheet is titled "Coffea arabica: Coffee", its Common name(s) line reads "coffee; Arabian coffee; coffee plant", and its Introduction opens "Arabian coffee is an economically important plant to many countries". Arabian Coffee is used here: it is RHS's lead name, the first entry of NC State's list and the opener of UF/IFAS's Introduction. The batch researched it as Coffee Plant, NC State's Description opener and the last entry in both NC State's and UF/IFAS's lists.
records.toxicity_detail: No admissible source names Coffea arabica in connection with cats or dogs, so toxic_to_pets is left null: NC State's page for this species has no Poison section, RHS's dedicated page has no Potentially harmful entry, and UF/IFAS's FPS135 fact sheet says nothing about toxicity. ASPCA's "Coffee Tree" entry is Polyscias guilfoylei, not this species, and none of it is imported. Edibility is conditional per NC State's Edibility field: "Fruits are edible, but seeds are what are usually dried, roasted and ground to make coffee. Coffee, of course, contains caffeine." The same page's Description says the berries are picked by hand when ripe and de-pulped, with the extracted beans then dried in the sun before roasting and grinding. UF/IFAS's Fruit characteristic field reads 'persists on the plant; suited for human consumption; showy'. NC State Plant Type tags: Edible, Shrub, Tree. Fruit Value To Gardener: Edible, Showy.
unknowns: The research pass could read only NC State's dedicated page. Three more admissible dedicated pages for Coffea arabica were read live at audit on 2026-10-07: RHS (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/4159/coffea-arabica/details), UF/IFAS fact sheet FPS135 (https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/FP135, which redirects to ask.ifas.ufl.edu) and MoBot (https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=b632, which redirects to plantfinder.mobot.org; that host fails for scripted clients and refuses this machine, so it was read in a browser by the auditor and nothing from it is cited). RHS's Position (Partial shade) and Moisture (Moist but well–drained), MoBot's Sun (Part shade), Culture temperatures (70-80°F day, 60-65°F night, leaf drop below 55°F) and size (6.00 to 15.00 feet), and UF/IFAS's Light requirement (plant grows in partial shade) and size (6 to 15 feet) agree with the values here; RHS's Max Height 4-8 metres and Max Spread 2.5-4 metres are larger, and MoBot's structured Water field reads Medium beside its Culture prose 'Keep soils consistently moist but not soggy.' A failed page is reported here and was not repaired or cached by hand.

toxic_to_pets is null: no admissible page names Coffea arabica with cats or dogs. NC State's page has no Poison section and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs or non-toxic tag; RHS's dedicated page has no Potentially harmful entry; UF/IFAS FPS135 says nothing about toxicity. ASPCA's 'Coffee Tree' is Polyscias guilfoylei, so its toxicity is not imported. Caffeine content is stated only as 'Coffee, of course, contains caffeine' in NC State's Edibility field, which names no animal and is not a pet-toxicity statement, so it cannot set toxic_to_pets either way.

is_edible is true but conditional: NC State says fruits are edible, while seeds are what are usually dried, roasted and ground to make coffee, and coffee contains caffeine. MoBot ('Berries are edible with a pulpy grape-like texture, but it is the seeds (coffee beans) that are coveted.'; not cited, browser read) and UF/IFAS (Fruit characteristic: 'persists on the plant; suited for human consumption; showy') agree; no admissible source disagrees on edibility.

mature_height_in and mature_spread_in (72-180 in) come from NC State's Dimensions block (Height and Width 6 ft. 0 in. - 15 ft. 0 in.), which states no growing context; MoBot (Height and Spread 6.00 to 15.00 feet; not cited, browser read) and UF/IFAS (Height and Spread 6 to 15 feet) agree, while RHS gives Max Height 4-8 metres and Max Spread 2.5-4 metres. NC State's prose says indoor plants are usually kept at a height of 4 to 6 feet (48-72 in), and MoBot says indoor container plants typically grow to about 4-6 feet; that indoor range is not entered in the fields, which carry the Dimensions block. NC State also says most coffee plantations trim the plants to 6 feet for ease of harvest.

water_regime keep_moist is read from NC State's prose 'kept consistently moist but not soggy'; its structured Soil Drainage tags are Good Drainage and Moist, which map to moderate drainage, not moisture_retentive. No source states a dry-down target, check depth or day interval, so those are null.

Soil pH: NC State lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0). The Acid band is open-ended, so no floor is set. RHS's pH field reads Acid or Neutral, with no alkaline entry, and UF/IFAS's Soil tolerances line reads 'acidic; loam'; soil_ph_max is left null rather than read off the closed 8.0 top of NC State's Neutral band.

direct_sun_hours_max is null: the only hour figure (2-6 hours) is inside NC State's generic Partial Shade light-category legend, not species-specific prose. outdoor_sun_exposure part_shade comes from NC State's Dappled Sunlight and Partial Shade tags plus the prose 'prefers some partial shade'.

chill_damage_f 55 is NC State's prose onset figure for leaf drop ('leaf drop can occur at temperatures below 55°F'); the same page's hardiness zones 10a-12b are a survival rating and were not used as an onset temperature.
Fertilizer: NC State only says to fertilize during the growing season, indoors or outdoors, with no interval, strength or named months, so the fertilize fields are null.

attracts_pollinators is null: NC State's page has no Attracts field and no pollinator statement (it lists fragrant, showy white flowers only). Light in foot-candles and humidity percentages are not stated by any page I could read.
Hardiness: NC State USDA zones 10a-12b; this is a tropical plant grown as a houseplant or conservatory plant in temperate areas, which affects the outdoor interpretation of any outdoor-only field.
